Pronounce
pro-nounce´
v. (to utter formally, to declare a verdict; rendering Hebrew bata, tame/taher in the causative, Greek apophthengomai)
From Latin pronuntiare, to announce publicly. In Leviticus the word is judicial: the priest does not cause the condition, he declares it.

Biblical Definition

Pronounce is one of the most doctrinally loaded verbs in the Old Testament, because of what the priest does in Leviticus 13. He examines the plague and then “pronounce[s] him unclean” (Lev 13:3) or “pronounce[s] him clean” (Lev 13:6). The priest does not heal the leper or infect him; he inspects and declares, and his declaration determines the man's standing in the camp. This is the exact grammar of justification: a forensic pronouncement about a person's status, made by one with authority to make it, on the basis of what is actually there. Leviticus even records the strange case where total coverage yields a clean verdict — “if the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean” (Lev 13:13) — the man who admits the disease entirely is the man declared clean. The word also warns about rash speech: whatever a man “shall pronounce with an oath” binds him even when forgotten (Lev 5:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pronounce as to speak, to utter articulately, and then as to utter formally, officially or solemnly — as to pronounce sentence or a decree.

expand to see more

PRONOUNCE, v.t. To speak; to utter articulately.

2. To utter formally, officially or solemnly.

Sentence is pronounced by the judge.

3. To speak or utter rhetorically; to deliver; as, to pronounce an oration. 4. To declare or affirm.

Key Scripture

Lev 13:3 — "And the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh: and when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean."

Lev 13:13 — "Then the priest shall consider: and, behold, if the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean that hath the plague: it is all turned white: he is clean."

Lev 13:6 — "And the priest shall look on him again the seventh day: and, behold, if the plague be somewhat dark, and the plague spread not in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean: it is but a scab: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean."

Lev 5:4 — "Or if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good, whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath, and it be hid from him; when he knoweth of it, then he shall be guilty in one of these."

Modern Corruption

Justification recast as a transformation God works inside a man rather than a verdict God pronounces over him — the Roman error the Reformation answered, and the priest of Leviticus 13 settles.

expand to see more

The Reformation controversy over justification turns on precisely this verb. Rome teaches an infused righteousness — God makes a man righteous and then accepts him. The Reformed position, following Paul, is that God pronounces the ungodly righteous on the ground of Christ's imputed obedience, and that the pronouncement is not a legal fiction but a true verdict about a real transfer. Leviticus 13 supplies the grammar in advance: the priest's word does not create the condition, and it absolutely determines the standing. Justification is a courtroom word, not a clinic word.

Leviticus 13:13 is the verse to press, because it is so counter-intuitive that it can only be deliberate. Partial leprosy leaves a man unclean; leprosy that has covered all his flesh yields the verdict clean. The man who can still point to healthy skin is shut up; the man wholly consumed by it is declared clean and sent home. That is total depravity and free justification pictured in a skin disease, and it is why the gospel is heard as good news only by those who have stopped negotiating about how much of them is still sound.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tame (H2930) in the causative, to declare unclean, and taher (H2891), to declare clean — both used of the priest's verdict; bata (H981), to speak rashly.

expand to see more

Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or declare unclean; in Lev 13 the causative form is a verdict, not an infection.

Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be or declare clean; the priest pronounces clean the man wholly covered (Lev 13:13).

Hebrew bata (H981) — to speak rashly, babble; the oath pronounced with the lips and forgotten, which still binds (Lev 5:4).

Usage

"“The priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean” — a verdict, not a cause."

"“If the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean” — total admission, clean verdict."

"“Whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath” — rash words still bind."
